messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 64

He is 80 now, a widowed South Asian man who spent most of his adult life in the Coast Guard, and when he begins talking about what happened, he does so with the same careful precision he once used on deck. He says the sea taught him that one careless moment can follow a man longer than any storm. He is not speaking metaphorically. Even now, decades later, that moment remains the point around which the rest of his life seems to organize itself.

At the time, he is in his thirties and already known as steady, competent, the sort of man younger crew members trust. He takes pride in being disciplined, in doing things properly, in never bringing panic to a tense situation. During a rough-weather operation, everything is moving quickly—orders, equipment, bodies shifting with the deck. He remembers noise first: the engine, shouted instructions, metal striking metal. Then one small mistake, his mistake. He handles a line too quickly, misjudges the timing, and another crewman is caught in the movement. The injury is severe. He still sees the man going down, still hears the sound that follows. In his memory, time slows cruelly around the instant before impact, as if there had been one final chance to stop it.

The injured man survives, but the survival does not soften what happened for him. In the immediate aftermath, he functions as he has been trained to function. He helps secure the scene, follows procedures, answers questions. Others tell him it was an accident, that conditions were bad, that anyone could have made the same error. He hears them, but their words do not enter him. Inside, something hardens into certainty: I did this. I ruined a man’s life because I was careless for one second.

He returns to duty, but the sea is no longer only the sea. Every rope, winch, and sudden command carries danger. He becomes meticulous beyond what the job requires, checking and rechecking equipment until others tease him about it. He laughs with them, but his body never loosens. He startles at sharp noises. When younger men move too casually around heavy gear, he snaps at them with a force that surprises even him. He tells himself he is protecting them. Secretly, he is trying to undo what cannot be undone.

At night, the scene replays. Sometimes in dreams he sees the injured crewman’s face; sometimes the dream is only motion and sound and the sickening certainty that he is too late. He wakes drenched in sweat, breathing hard, his heart racing as though he is back on deck. In the dark beside his wife, he lies still and waits for his pulse to slow. He does not wake her. In the morning he is quiet, already tired, irritable over small things. She asks what troubles him, and he shrugs, says work is work. He comes from a family and a culture where a man is expected to carry his burdens without spilling them into the room.

As the years pass, he builds a life that looks solid from the outside. He continues his service. He raises children. He pays bills, attends weddings, fixes things around the house, keeps his shoes lined neatly by the door. Yet the accident remains just below the surface. He avoids reunions if he thinks someone might mention it. He cannot tolerate films or news stories showing industrial injuries. If he sees a dockside accident on television, he changes the channel immediately, then sits tense and distracted for the rest of the evening. His wife learns there are certain questions not to ask.

What troubles him most is not fear alone but shame. He has spent years believing he does not deserve the comfort he has. When his children are young and run toward him noisily, a flash of alarm passes through him before affection can arrive. He is watchful in ordinary situations, scanning for hazards, calculating how quickly harm can happen. Even after retirement, his body behaves as if catastrophe is one inattention away. He patrols his home the way he once inspected a vessel—doors locked, stove checked twice, tools put away so no one can get hurt.

After his wife dies, the structure that helped contain him falls away. The nights lengthen. With no one beside him, he has fewer reasons to keep the memories at bay. He sleeps in fragments. Sometimes he dozes in a chair and wakes convinced he has heard the clatter of equipment and a man crying out. He avoids the waterfront, though he once loved walking there. On some mornings he feels heavy with dread before he has even stood up. He tells himself he is an old man thinking too much, but the guilt remains young, sharp, unchanged.

Now, when he speaks about the injured crewman, he does not use the man’s name at first. It is as if naming him would make the memory fully present in the room. He rubs his palms together and looks down, embarrassed by the force of his own emotion. He says he knows, logically, that it was an accident. He has known that for many years. But logic has never touched the image that lives inside him: one second, one mistake, another man’s body breaking because of his hands. Even at 80, he lives with the feeling that he must stay vigilant, must not relax, because the cost of one ordinary human error is far too high.
